28:4.text: The LORD was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.

provenance.other: “Mourning and lamentation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 2:5. “Great mourning” occurs in three — Esther 4:3, Zechariah 12:11 and Matthew 2:18 — and Zechariah 12:11 is the one that also stands at the head of the family-by-family list this chapter's next verse imitates.
provenance.significance: Recover Lamentations 2:5 and the clause that produced the phrase reads “The LORD was as an enemy.” Alma 28 has just narrated a battle won by the Nephites, and it declines to call the day a victory: it calls it a sorrowful day. Borrowing the grief-word of the KJV's one poem about a city destroyed by God's own hand imports the theology of that poem — that a slaughter is a visitation before it is a military event — into a chapter whose own explicit moral, four verses later, is that the war has produced nothing but an awful scene of bloodshed.

28:4.note: “A great mourning and lamentation heard throughout all the land.” The compound is a KJV singleton and its home is Lamentations 2, where it is what the LORD “increased in the daughter of Judah” after breaking her strong holds. Mosiah 21:9 used the same singleton for the mourning of Limhi's people, and the recurrence is worth naming: the same editorial hand reaches for the same verse whenever a Nephite army has been cut to pieces. Written as a fresh link rather than a repeat because this is a new book and a new narrative, but the argument was first made at Mosiah 21:9.

28:5.text: And the land shall mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart;

provenance.other: “Every family apart” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Zechariah 12:12 and 12:14, and the itemised-household form of mourning is confined to that passage. No other KJV lament breaks the grief down by relation.
provenance.alternative: National mourning enumerated by kinship is a natural way to write the scene and needs no source; the shared words are only 'mourn' and the family terms.
provenance.significance: Zechariah's family-by-family mourning is for one who was pierced — “they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son.” Alma 28 puts the form to the opposite use: the households here mourn not one death that saves but tens of thousands that accomplish nothing, and verse 11 says outright that many of the mourned are “consigned to a state of endless wo.” The KJV's one liturgy of universal household grief is being run in reverse.

28:5.note: “The cry of widows mourning for their husbands, and also of fathers mourning for their sons, and the daughter for the brother; yea, the brother for the father.” The verbal contact is thin — mourning, and the kinship terms — but the form is distinctive and the KJV has one instance of it: Zechariah 12:12-14, where the land mourns “every family apart,” household by household, wives apart. Recorded at moderate on form rather than wording, and paired with the Lamentations 2:5 singleton in the preceding verse, which comes from the same kind of scene and which Mosiah 21:9 had already fused with this same Zechariah passage.

28:6.text: Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.

provenance.other: “Fasting and prayer,” in that order, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 7:5. The reversed “prayer and fasting” occurs in two, Matthew 17:21 and Mark 9:29. 1 Corinthians 7:5 is also the only one of the three that sets the practice inside a bounded stretch of time — “except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer” — which is the construction Alma 28:6 has.
provenance.alternative: Fasting and prayer is one of the most ordinary pairs in devotional English and the order may carry nothing.
provenance.significance: The order is the whole of the evidence, and it is worth having for that reason: where the Book of Mormon reproduces a KJV word-pair it tends to reproduce the pair as the KJV set it, and here the sequence it has is Paul's, not the Gospels'. Recovering 1 Corinthians 7:5 supplies a small irony the chapter did not ask for — Paul's time of fasting and prayer is a season husbands and wives agree to spend apart, and the mourning this one answers is, in the previous verse, first of all the cry of widows for their husbands.

28:6.note: “A time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer.” A four-word run against a KJV singleton, and the only KJV verse to hold “a time” and “fasting and prayer” together. The case is entirely about word order, since the sense of 1 Corinthians 7:5 is remote; held at moderate for that reason.
28:6.whyNot: The sense of the source is marital continence, which has nothing to do with a nation fasting after a battle, and a writer with any KJV in his ear could produce this order without 1 Corinthians 7:5.

28:8.text: Thus saith the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the LORD that is faithful, and the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee.

provenance.other: “The Lord, the Redeemer of …” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 49:7, where the genitive is “of Israel.” The same clause stands verbatim in the Book of Mormon's own transcription of Isaiah 49 at 1 Nephi 21:7, so the proximate model cannot be discriminated from the KJV by wording; what can be said is that the phrase was already inside the corpus and available to be altered.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 49:7 in the KJV, without the intervening Book of Mormon transcription, would explain the wording equally well.
provenance.significance: The one word changed is the argument. Isaiah's title is “the Redeemer of Israel”; Alma 28:8 makes it “the Redeemer of all men,” and does so in the sentence that closes the account of a mission to the Lamanites — the nation a Nephite reader has been taught to regard as outside. Recover Isaiah 49:7 and the rest of the verse turns out to describe precisely the missionaries being blessed: it addresses “him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers,” and promises that “Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship.” Ammon and his brethren spent these chapters despised, imprisoned, servants to rulers, and watching two Lamanite kings rise and worship. The chapter's benediction is worded out of the one Isaiah verse whose contents it has just narrated.

28:8.note: “And now may the Lord, the Redeemer of all men, bless their souls forever.” A KJV singleton clause with one substitution: Israel becomes all men. The substitution is not decorative — it is the doctrinal conclusion of the Ammon narrative stated as a divine title, and it is made on a verse the Book of Mormon has already reproduced word for word at 1 Nephi 21:7, where it still reads “of Israel.” Mediation is given as OT-via-earlier-BoM on that ground, with the caveat in provenance that the two routes are verbally identical here.

28:8.text: In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 11:26 and 6:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Journeyings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Numbers 10:28 and 2 Corinthians 11:26; “in journeyings often” is a singleton at 2 Corinthians 11:26. “As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing” is a singleton at 2 Corinthians 6:10.
provenance.alternative: A summary colophon naturally lists what a narrative contained, and the items listed are what Alma 17-27 in fact narrated.
provenance.significance: Recover the source and what Alma 28:8 has borrowed is not a phrase but a genre: Paul's catalogue of missionary hardship, the peristasis list of 2 Corinthians 6:4-10 and 11:23-27, which is the New Testament's set form for a preacher summarising what his commission cost him. Its signature is the turn at the end — “as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing” — and Alma 28:8 ends its list the same way, with “their incomprehensible joy.” Verse 14 then names the antithesis in the abstract, “the great reason of sorrow, and also of rejoicing,” which is 2 Corinthians 6:10 unpacked.

28:8.note: “Their journeyings in the land of Nephi, their sufferings in the land, their sorrows, and their afflictions, and their incomprehensible joy.” The rare word is 'journeyings', which the KJV uses twice, once of Israel's marches and once in Paul's list of what apostleship cost him; the shape of the sentence is the second. Held at moderate because the individual words are common and the case rests on the form of the list plus the sorrow-and-joy turn that closes it — but the form is not a common one, and this is a missionary colophon, which is exactly where it belongs.

28:12.text: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.

provenance.other: “Right hand of God” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses — Mark 16:19, Acts 2:33, Acts 7:55, Acts 7:56, Romans 8:34, Colossians 3:1, Hebrews 10:12, 1 Peter 3:22 — and in every one of the eight the occupant of that place is Christ. No KJV verse puts anyone else there.
provenance.alternative: Romans 8:34, which the machine stream ranked first, joins 'risen again' to 'the right hand of God' as tightly as Colossians 3:1 does, and the two cannot be separated on wording.
provenance.significance: The interest of the row is not which of the eight verses is in view but that the Book of Mormon has moved the seat. The KJV reserves the right hand of God for the risen Christ; Alma 28:12 has ordinary Nephite dead “raised to dwell at the right hand of God.” The only KJV licence for that transfer is the participatory logic of Colossians 3:1 — 'if ye then be risen with Christ' — where the believer's resurrection and Christ's session are the same fact seen twice. Alma 28:12 states as the destination of the faithful dead what Colossians states as a present standing.

28:12.note: “They are raised to dwell at the right hand of God, in a state of never ending happiness.” “Right hand of God” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and is too widely spread to fix a source on its own, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion; what is not widely spread is the combination of being raised and being at that right hand, which the KJV has at Colossians 3:1 and Romans 8:34 alone, and only Colossians extends the position to anyone but Christ.
28:12.whyNot: Eight KJV verses carry the phrase and the wording here matches none of them beyond it; a reader may reasonably treat the expression as general Christian idiom rather than dependence on any one verse.

28:14.text: For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.

provenance.route: Matthew 20:1 (with Isaiah 5:7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Labourers into his vineyard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:1; “the vineyard of the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:7. Alma 28:14's “labor in the vineyards of the Lord” fuses the two and matches neither exactly. “In the vineyards of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Song of Solomon 1:14, the vineyards of Engedi, which is registered as an exclusion at this verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 5:7 defines whose vineyard it is — “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” — and Matthew 20:1 supplies the labourers hired into it. Put them together and the metaphor Alma 28:14 uses for missionary work carries both halves: the field being worked is Israel, which is exactly the claim Alma 17-27 has been making about the Lamanites, and the labourers are hired at every hour, which is Matthew 20's point and the point of a chapter that has just watched an enemy nation come in late.

28:14.note: “The great call of diligence of men to labor in the vineyards of the Lord.” Neither KJV phrase is reproduced intact, which is what keeps this at moderate; but labouring in a vineyard belonging to the Lord is a fusion of two singletons and not a free-standing image, and Jacob 5 had already built the Book of Mormon's longest allegory out of the same two sources. Written as a link rather than a recurrence because Jacob is another book and another hand.

28:14.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

provenance.other: “Light of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:12. The Book of Mormon's clause “the light of Christ unto life” splits the singleton and inserts the name that John 8:12 only implies.
provenance.significance: John 8:12 is a self-identification — “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” — and its two halves are darkness and life. Alma 28:14 sets its borrowing against exactly that pair: “sorrow because of death and destruction among men, and joy because of the light of Christ unto life.” The chapter has spent eleven verses on bodies mouldering in heaps, and it closes by naming the one KJV verse in which light and life are a single phrase and the alternative to them is walking in the dark.

28:14.note: “Joy because of the light of Christ unto life.” The KJV joins 'light' to 'life' in one verse only, and the Book of Mormon has that verse's phrase with Christ's name written into the middle of it — the identification John 8:12 makes in its first clause moved into the second. The antithesis of death against light-and-life in the same sentence is John 8:12's own.
